item.title: The Scientist Who Kickstarted Pennsylvania’s Fracking Boom Thought Gas Would Be a ‘Bridge Fuel’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth analysis of a significant environmental issue with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

Almost 20 years ago, a Penn State University geoscientist named Terry Engelder published an eye-popping estimate of the volume of gas sitting beneath Pennsylvania. It’s now the second-biggest producer of gas in the U.S., behind only Texas.

At the time, Engelder says now, he hoped that his assessment would help to curb greenhouse gas emissions because it would encourage the transition away from coal. But he now fears that natural gas has become a long-term occupant of the energy landscape rather than the “bridge fuel” that he and others thought they were promoting.

Engelder, now an emeritus professor of geology at Penn State, is writing a book describing his work in estimating that the Marcellus Shale deposit—which also underlies parts of West Virginia, New York and Ohio—had enough gas to meet total U.S. needs for about 20 years under consumption rates at the time.

Engelder’s estimate of 489 trillion cubic feet (tcf) of technically recoverable gas—published in 2009, and still, he says, underlying industry assumptions today—first persuaded bankers to lend the energy industry billions of dollars to extract the gas using hydraulic fracturing of mile-deep shale beds. Critics say the process causes environmental and public health harms, adds to global emissions and that its entrenchment in Pennsylvania has stunted the growth of renewables.

His estimate was broadly confirmed by the U.S. Energy Information Administration, which in 2011 estimated the Marcellus contained 410 tcf of gas. In 2018, it was revised upward by the University of Texas, which calculated the field had about 560 tcf of technically recoverable gas.

Engelder hoped natural gas, which creates about 55 percent of the carbon emissions of coal, would act as a transition on the way to a renewable-dominated future. But with its increasing use since the start of the fracking revolution in Pennsylvania, its status is now at odds with Engelder’s original vision. Almost 60 percent of Pennsylvania’s electricity now comes from gas.

Demand for natural gas is expected to increase further, driven by energy-hungry data centers, dozens of which are planned for Pennsylvania.

“I really was optimistic that wind and solar were going to become American industries, and America was going to have the best solar cells, and that gas was going to serve as a bridge fuel,” Engelder said, in an interview with Inside Climate News. “It turns out that it’s become more of a permanent feature than a bridge fuel.”

Engelder described how he calculated the size of the Marcellus reserve, and how he hoped its exploitation would help slow climate change by encouraging the use of natural gas rather than coal. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. .

JON HURDLE: In making your estimate of the huge amount of natural gas in the Marcellus, were you motivated by the idea that increased use of natural gas rather than coal would help to reduce carbon emissions?

TERRY ENGELDER: Absolutely. The most low-hanging fruit in terms of slowing the American rate of injection to the atmosphere was that conversion of coal to natural gas. That conversion, particularly in places like Pennsylvania, had a huge impact. Probably the most important thing my calculation did was it rapidly made the rate of CO2 being added to the atmosphere go down.

HURDLE: Do you have any qualms about providing the information that the industry needed to exploit the vast reserves that it has done so far?

ENGELDER: Evidence of my concern about climate change is shown in a TED Talk I gave in 2013 in which I said I had to make the judgment between furthering the era of fossil fuels, and trying to get into a position where climate change could be dealt with.

HURDLE: Did you try to reconcile those positions described in the TED Talk?

ENGELDER: These two positions just can’t be reconciled. This was always a scientific Sophie’s choice. It still is the type of choice for most, if not all, geologists who work in industry. They all know the terrible choice they are making.

HURDLE: What prompted you to do the estimate?

ENGELDER: These [fracking] companies were asking for billions of dollars; it was non-trivial money. Banks weren’t going to give these companies billions of dollars without some sort of outside confirmation that these companies were actually on the right track. I gave a webinar in 2007 to a bunch of the banks that included Morgan Stanley and Deutsche Bank. One of the bankers asked, “How much gas is there in the Marcellus? How much can be recovered for our billions of dollars?” That led to my calculation.

Suddenly, the banks freed up a lot of money for companies like Chesapeake and Range and Anadarko.

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

HURDLE: How did you calculate the 489 tcf number?

ENGELDER: By using production data from Pennsylvania, Ohio and West Virginia from the end of 2008. That number has held up for a decade and a half now.

HURDLE: Did you make earlier estimates?

ENGELDER: Yes, I came up with a number which was, I thought, incredibly large. At the time, it was 363 trillion cubic feet. I said: “This is too large; I don’t need to tell anyone it’s that large. They might not believe me.” So the first number was 50 tcf, published on Jan. 17, 2008, but it was not based on production data because there weren’t any yet. The 50 tcf estimate was arbitrary. It could have been 100 tcf.

HURDLE: How much public interest was there in your estimate at the time?…

item.title: ‘Sinking’ African megacities will expose seven million people to flooding by 2050
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important research on a critical environmental issue with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

‘Sinking’ African megacities will expose seven million people to flooding by 2050

Sinking land and rising seas could expose more than seven million people living in Africa’s coastal “megacities” to flooding by the middle of the century, according to new research.

The analysis, published in Science Advances, combines satellite data with projections of sea level rise to assess the risk of flooding in 20 of Africa’s most populous coastal cities.

The study finds that, under a moderate warming scenario, an “extreme sea level event” – when sea levels are unusually high due to short-term changes in weather and ocean conditions – could expose a million buildings and $180bn of assets to flooding.

Lagos, the capital of Nigeria, and Alexandria in Egypt are the most vulnerable cities in the analysis.

In these two cities alone, five million people and $150bn in assets could be exposed to flooding and the cities by mid-century.

Human activity, such as pumping groundwater or drilling for fossil fuels, can cause the ground to sink, in a process called “subsidence”.

Seismic or volcanic activity can also drive changes in the height of the land, causing it to either rise or fall. This “vertical land movement” can either alleviate or exacerbate the effects of sea level rise.

The researchers combined more than 4,000 satellite images of Africa’s coastline to determine how quickly different regions are rising or sinking.

They identified Lagos and Alexandria as “subsidence hotspots”, finding that the two cities are sinking at rates of 5.2mm and 6.3mm per year, respectively.

This is “comparable to rates reported for south-east Asian megacities such as Jakarta, Manila and Ho Chi Minh City”, which have recorded “some of the highest subsidence rates yet observed”, according to the study.

The authors combined these estimates with sea level rise projections from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s sixth assessment report under three different emissions scenarios, to assess the regional sea level rise across the African coastline.

They used 2020 population data, building footprints and GDP per capita to estimate how much of each city would be exposed to these flooding events over the 21st century, if the city itself stays the same.

While Lagos and Alexandria are the most vulnerable cities, the research finds that Djibouti City in Djibouti, Mogadishu in Somalia and Tripoli in Libya will face “minimal economic exposure due to their smaller populations and infrastructure bases”.

Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho, a PhD student at Virginia Tech, tells Carbon Brief that the analysis holds population and city data constant at 2020 levels, so that the authors can isolate the effects of sea level rise and vertical land movement on changing flood exposure.

He notes that if people move away from “threatened areas” over the coming decades, then estimates could be too high. However, if “continued urban growth” causes city populations to increase, the estimates could be too low.

Africa is the world’s fastest-urbanising region, with cities growing at an average rate of 3.5% every year. By 2050, Africa’s urban population is expected to double from 7m to 1.4bn.

He also notes that “the flood model assumes no coastal defenses, so the estimates are a worst-case physical picture”.

Subsidence in African coastal cities has not been consistently monitored in the past, largely due to a lack of local data, the study explains.

The authors say their method of using satellites to assess subsidence and uplift could be used in other “data-scarce coastal regions across the global south”.

Dasho, O., et al (2026), Sinking cities: Latent flood risk in Africa’s coastal megacities, Science Advances, doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh6538

Source: Carbon Brief | Published: 2026-11-27 19:00 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://www.carbonbrief.org/sinking-african-megacities-will-expose-seven-million-people-to-flooding-by-2050

item.title: Refugee families use agroforestry to restore degraded landscape in Bangladesh camp
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging story with clear reporting and useful vocabulary on environmental restoration efforts.

- After the 2017 influx, over 1,500 hectares of protected forest in Cox’s Bazar were cleared to build refugee shelters, stripping the hillsides of vegetation and triggering a crisis of deadly landslides and soil erosion.

- Rohingya refugees are using traditional agroecology techniques on agroforestry plots, such as multi-layered intercropping, organic composting, and seed saving, to heal the degraded landscape and grow food amid deep cuts to international food aid.

- Supported by NGOs like UNHCR and FAO, large-scale reforestation projects have planted nearly one million tree seedlings and restored 200 hectares of camp land, using a mix of fast-growing species and deep-rooted native trees, including fruit trees, to stabilize the sandy slopes and prevent landslides.

- While reforestation efforts in the camp are showing measurable success, the long-term survival of forests is impacted by funding shortages and a lack of secure land rights for refugees.

KUTUPALONG REFUGEE CAMP, Bangladesh —”It is like a jail, but it isn’t a jail,” says Roshid Ahamed Bin, a 47-year-old Rohingya farmer, living in what is now a refugee camp in Bangladesh. It is far from the farmland where he used to live in Myanmar, before he and thousands of Rohingya people like him fled persecution eight years ago.

Here, amid the world’s largest refugee settlement with over 1.1 million refugees, space is tight and evergreen forests have paid the price. But families are combining NGO-funded farming projects with traditional Rohingya agroecology techniques to create agroforestry plots that are restoring land while helping refugees become self-sufficient in response to deep cuts in international food aid.

“I feel so bad here as I have no land, but I am keeping my ancestors’ heritage alive. Growing these crops reminds me of the life we had in Myanmar. Here, life is difficult,” said Amina Khatun, a 58-year-old refugee living in Camp 1W, a sector of the sprawling settlement.

Before the 2017 influx, Kutupalong refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar was a tropical evergreen forest, dominated by Dipterocarpus species, and sanctuary for endangered Asian elephants (Elephas maximus). To make way for the massive refugee settlements, the Bangladeshi government allocated roughly 2,500 hectares (6,100 acres) of protected forest land, and refugees and aid agencies cleared the vegetation to build shelters and provide firewood. Over 1,500 hectares of forest were cleared in total.

The rain, with nowhere to soak in, ran straight down the slopes. Landslides became a seasonal terror, sources told Mongabay.

But in the past several years, on the hillsides where there was once bare, sandy earth and the blue-black glare of tarpaulin, there are now nurseries and gardens. Across the camps, more than 159,000 refugees are engaged in homestead gardening. Space is severely limited, and not all use agroecology techniques. Some farmers rely on chemical sprays and paddy fields to make ends meet.

But among them, there are traditional food gardens and permaculture designs that avoid synthetic pesticides entirely, relying instead on intercropping, a mix of trees and organic soil management.

Knowledge that crossed the border

Mongabay sat with Roshid Ahamed Bin inside Camp 27. He remembers the farmland in Rakhine state, Myanmar, before 2017.

Despite the confinement of the camp, Ahamed Bin has found a way to reconnect with the life he left behind. Like many Rohingya refugees here, he was a farmer in Myanmar. Now, he is among a growing number of refugees using agroforestry to restore the camp’s degraded landscape and feed their families.

“Our land may be far away, but the farming passion of our ancestors remains part of our lives,” he told Mongabay.

Back in Myanmar, farming was not just a livelihood for his family, but a way of life rooted in the land. His family grew rice, vegetables, and fruit, using layered intercropping and agroforestry. They planted local varieties of banana, papaya, and mango trees directly beside their vegetable gardens to maximize space and provide shade. They removed insects by hand, added animal manure and composted leaves to keep the soil alive, and saved seeds from healthy crops.

Several U.N. agencies and NGOs are providing support to these efforts and they actively integrate Rohingya traditional knowledge into their programs. The UNHCR SuLMER project has rehabilitated the Shoa Ma’r Jhiri stream, stabilized slopes, and introduced kitchen gardens, relying on community input to decide what to plant. CARE’s training in ‘sack and vertical gardening’ builds on the Rohingya tradition of maximizing tiny spaces. Similarly, when FAO and WFP distribute seeds, they rely on the refugees’ traditional knowledge of seed-saving and intercropping. Together, these programs have engaged tens of thousands of refugees.

“They have skills in planting, fertilizer, pest control, harvesting, timing,” said Jahir Ahamed, a staffer at the UNHCR SuLMER prokect. “We use suitable practices in gardening activities.”

Because families like his fled so quickly, they didn’t bring their own seeds from Myanmar and rely on those from distributed. They grow many leafy vegetables and gourds, like amaranth and Indian spinach.

Mabia Khatun, 38, from Camp 17, recalls her own farm practices. “We saved seeds from healthy plants,” she said. A practice, they still engage in with seeds provided by NGOs. “Sometimes we exchanged seeds with neighbors. Our elders taught us to care for plants and protect the land.”

According to FAO and UNHCR reports, the restoration involves a mix of fast-growing tree species for quick ground cover and slower native species for long-term slope stability. On the ground, this looks like multi-layered intercropping.

This method is highly strategic for the camp’s harsh environment. By stacking plants of different heights together, families can grow food in tiny spaces while the deep roots hold the sandy soil in place.…

Source: Mongabay | Published: 2026-11-27 15:32 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: In Republic of Congo, residents and a scientist take on a fight against lead pollution
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed account of a local environmental issue with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

- Nearly 120 residents of Vindoulou, a neighborhood in Pointe-Noire in the Republic of Congo, filed a civil claim in October 2026, seeking compensation and medical care after years of suspected lead exposure allegedly linked to the Metssa Congo battery recycling plant.

- Blood tests conducted in 2023 with support from Amnesty International found lead levels in the blood samples of residents, including children, far above the WHO’s reference level.

- In 2026, residents worked with Columbia University researcher Alexander Van Geen to test soil around the former plant: Of 49 samples, 41% exceeded the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s threshold for safe levels for residential soil where children play.

- Although the plant closed in 2024, residents say no cleanup has taken place and researchers say that the contamination is serious but geographically limited.

Nearly 120 residents of Vindoulou, a neighborhood in Pointe-Noire, Republic of Congo, have filed a civil claim before the city’s High Court in relation to pollution allegedly caused by a foundry.

“We want tests, but also compensation for damages and losses,” Cyrille Traoré Ndembi, a plaintiff and president of the Vindoulou Residents’ Collective, which represents people living in the working-class neighborhood, told Mongabay on the phone.

The civil case, filed in October, is the latest in a series of actions taken against Metssa Congo, a foundry that opened in the neighborhood in 2013.The facility recycled, among other things, car batteries, extracting lead and turning it into lead bars for export. The plant is part of the Metssa Group, an industrial metals trading company based in the United Arab Emirates.

The battery recycling process can pose serious health risks. According to the WHO, lead can be released in the form of fumes, particles and dust at every stage of the process, from draining and dismantling to smelting and refining. Environmental contamination from recycling can be substantial, exposing workers and nearby communities to significant levels of lead, the health agency says on its website.

According to Traore Ndembi, residents of Vindoulou soon experienced this reality first-hand, complaining about toxic fumes coming from the plant. In 2019, they decided to register their discontent over pollution.

“We wrote to the public authorities, to the departmental director of health,” Traoré Ndembi said. “We also wrote to the local environmental authorities but they said there was no pollution. The health authorities in the Kouilou department then carried out medical tests like chest X-rays to prove that the area was not polluted. Their findings said we were not sick, that there was nothing wrong. So we decided to take matters into our own hands.”

To provide scientific evidence to support their complaint, in 2023 the communities, with the help of NGO Amnesty International, conducted blood tests on a small group of residents, including both adults and children. The results were unequivocal: The people tested had blood lead levels far above the threshold recommended by the WHO, namely 5 micrograms per deciliter (µg/dL) or one-tenth of a liter. While there is no known level of safe exposure to lead, the health agency recommends taking action when levels cross this threshold. In some cases, the levels detected were 10 times higher.

The situation was alarming, according to the human rights organization, and the findings proved decisive for the communities. The residents’ collective won its first legal battle: The administrative court of Pointe-Noire ordered the company to suspend its operations and the government instructed the operator to fund site decontamination and medical care.

‘I can’t keep [the children] locked indoors’

Yet, two years later, Traoré Ndembi, who still lives in Vindoulou with his wife and children, remains worried.

“The authorities are not telling us anything,” he said. “It is true that the plant has closed, but nothing has changed on the ground since then. Nothing has been cleaned up. We are still living in an area that has been polluted for years.”

“Closing the plant is not enough. The medical test results confirmed that we had been poisoned by lead, so we need to receive medical care and treatment! And the plant must clean up and decontaminate the site,” he said. “Because what guarantees that, even though it has stopped operating, it is no longer polluting? I don’t feel at ease when my children play outside, but I can’t keep them locked indoors either.”

Alexander Van Geen, a research professor specialized in environmental contaminants and member of the Earth Institute faculty at Columbia University, told Mongabay in a phone interview for a previous article about possible contamination from the Metssa plant that he had been shocked by the blood test results obtained by Amnesty International. “I have to admit that when I first saw the data, I thought, ‘This can’t be possible.’,” he said. “I thought that at levels this high, children would be dying or suffering from terrible tremors. I was horrified.”

According to the WHO, exposure to lead is highly toxic and can cause lead poisoning, a serious condition that affects the brain, liver, kidneys and bones. The U.N. agency estimates that lead exposure caused more than 1.5 million deaths worldwide in 2021, mainly through cardiovascular effects. Aware of the scale of the problem, Van Geen told Mongabay in early 2026 that “something needs to be done.”

A new round of testing

His words were followed by action. After Mongabay published its article, he contacted Cyrille Traoré Ndembi and the Vindoulou Residents’ Collective to carry out another round of tests, this time on the soil.

“It was important to me that the affected communities carry out their own measurements,” he said after the new round of tests. “I thought that if blood lead levels were high, the lead had to be coming from somewhere. So, we began looking at the soil.”…

Source: Mongabay | Published: 2026-11-27 15:19 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: International Jaguar Day: Big cats hold on at the edges of their range
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Informative piece on the status of jaguars with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

International Jaguar Day has been marked every Nov. 29 since 2018, to raise awareness of the threats faced by the Americas’ biggest cats and the efforts to protect them.

Jaguars (Panthera onca) were once found across some 19 million square kilometers (7.3 million square miles), from what is today the southwestern U.S. to central Argentina.

But their range has shrunk by more than half, and today spans about 9 million km² (3.5 million mi²). Most jaguars live in a stronghold ranging from the Amazon Rainforest and stretching into the Pantanal wetlands, the Chaco dry forest and the Llanos grasslands of Colombia and Venezuela.

However, recent sightings and reports from outside these core areas highlight that many jaguars are still holding on at the edges of their historical territory.

For example, in Brazil’s eastern Atlantic Forest and dry Caatinga, fewer than 250 adult jaguars survive, and researchers have begun banking their genes in an effort to save them through cloning.

At the northern edge of the species’ range, a male nicknamed Cinco showed up on camera footage in southern Arizona state in late 2025, becoming the fifth jaguar recorded there in 15 years.

Meanwhile, in Honduras’s Sierra del Merendón, a mountain range in the country’s northwest, camera traps recorded a young male at an altitude of about 2,200 meters (7,200 feet) for the first time in a decade.

“The fact that they’re able to travel through these high elevation areas also shows how resilient they are,” Allison Devlin, who directs the jaguar program at the wildcat conservation NGO Panthera, told Mongabay’s Spoorthy Raman.

The Merendón mountains form a corridor between Honduras and Guatemala, allowing wildlife to move between the two countries.

“It reaffirms that there are dispersed populations in the northwestern part of the country,” said Marcio Martinez, a coordinator at Honduras’s National Institute of Forest Conservation.

Also in Honduras, authorities raided the home of a businessman in Olancho, in the east, and seized a female jaguar estimated to be about a year old, along with a capuchin monkey, two parrots and a python. The jaguar is thought to have been captured in the Mosquitia forests, a stronghold for the species.

The young cat now lives at a rehabilitation center run by the Honduran armed forces and may be returned to a protected area if considered fit enough.

Banner image: This female jaguar, kept as a pet by a businessman, was seized as part of a two-week-long operation. Image courtesy of the ICF Wildlife Department.

What kind of wealth do Borneo’s ancient rainforests hold?

Industries such as logging and palm oil have generated vast monetary wealth for some. But for the Indigenous communities who call the Malaysian Borneo home—its forests, rivers and mountains hold a different kind of value.

These forests are interconnected ecosystems that sustain communities with food, medicine and livelihoods, while holding generations of knowledge, traditions and culture.

But as industrial pressures continue to pressure these landscapes, some communities are working harder than ever to defend their homes and protect the ecological wealth that exists in these forests.

item.title: Aerial photos show recovery of Florida Bay, US, as restoration sends Everglades water
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Illustrative story of environmental restoration with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

- Freshwater flows into Florida Bay, significantly reduced by decades of Everglades drainage, are slowly increasing under the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan.

- Helicopter surveys by avian ecologist Mark Ian Cook document returning wading birds, wintering waterfowl, American flamingos and threatened American crocodiles.

- Wading bird nesting reached a record high in 2018 but has since declined, while a severe 2025–2026 drought underscored the birds’ sensitivity to water fluctuations.

From a low-flying helicopter above the coastal Everglades in southern Florida, U.S., Mark Ian Cook looks down at dense mangrove forests and silty shallows rarely seen by others. Below him, bottlenose dolphins trap mullet in rings of mud, nurse sharks mate in sheltered waters and flamingos forage on remote mudflats.

Cook, an avian ecologist who heads the South Florida Water Management District’s Everglades Research Group, tracks how wading birds respond to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan (CERP), a decades-long federal-state effort to return freshwater to the southern Everglades and Florida Bay. He conducts a flying survey about every two weeks during the birds’ breeding season, photographing nesting colonies through a small flap in the helicopter door.

Some colonies hold tens of thousands of nests, too many to count by eye, so photos are the most reliable way to tally them, he told Mongabay in a video call. His best frames also help persuade water managers. “My information was so much more effective when I had an image rather than just data or a boring old graph with counts on it,” he said. Cook said he has two advantages when capturing his images: an ecologist’s sense of where and when to find unusual animal behavior and wildlife events, and regular flights over thousands of square miles of remote subtropical wilderness.

His photos play with shape, color and texture, like a flock of lesser scaup (Aythya affinis) that briefly formed a pyramid on a coastal lake after returning in large numbers. Striking images hold a viewer’s attention longer, he said, and “while they’re trying to figure out what they’re looking at, they are more likely to soak in my conservation message.” In those moments, Cook sees nature as the artist and his job as “simply to recognize the art and frame it appropriately.”

Wading birds such as storks, ibises, spoonbills and herons respond quickly to water levels, making them good indicators of restoration. Historically, summer rains caused Lake Okeechobee, approximately 182 kilometers (113 miles) away, to overflow, sending a shallow, slow-moving sheet of water south across the Everglades — the so-called River of Grass — to Florida Bay. Here it mixed with seawater to create the brackish conditions the estuary’s fish, crocodiles and birds depend on.

In the 1930s and early 1940s, the region supported more than 200,000 nests, most along the coast, Cook said. Canals, levees and roads then significantly reduced the freshwater reaching Florida Bay and coastal nesting collapsed.

“When inches of water can make a huge difference in such a flat landscape, that just really affected everything,” Cook said.

Reversing that damage is CERP’s main objective. Authorized by the U.S. Congress in 2000, it is the largest environmental restoration program in the South Florida region, addressing the quantity, quality, timing and distribution of water, with healthy wading bird populations a central goal. The most recent report to Congress projects it will take about 50 years at a cost of $26.9 billion in 2023 dollars, equivalent to roughly $29.8 billion in 2026.

When Hurricane Irma dumped heavy rain across South Florida in 2017, enough freshwater flowed through the Everglades to reach the coast. South Florida recorded 138,834 wading bird nests in 2018, the most since system-wide surveys began in 1995 according to the South Florida Wading Bird Report, which Cook edits. Nests topped 100,000 again in 2021.

“The response was just amazing,” Cook said. “The wading birds came back in really high numbers.”

Other species are rebounding too. American crocodile (Crocodylus acutus) populations are increasing, as are waterfowl numbers. In 2024, tens of thousands of waterfowl, including blue-winged teal (Spatula discors) and lesser scaup, returned to the area’s coastal lakes in concentrations not seen in roughly 80 years. American flamingos, hunted out of Florida more than a century ago, are back as wintering birds. They haven’t nested yet, but “even if they don’t nest, that doesn’t mean that they’re not native,” Cook said.

But progress has been uneven. After exceptional nesting seasons in 2018 and 2021, wading bird nesting has declined for several consecutive years. In 2025, drought contributed to the lowest nesting levels recorded in roughly 30 years in Everglades National Park, according to a recent wading bird report. Rising seas have also cut Florida Bay’s roseate spoonbill (Platalea ajaja) nests from about 400 in 2012 to 157 in 2022, even as the birds have established new nesting colonies farther north in Florida.

Storage remains a bottleneck: Without room to hold Lake Okeechobee’s excess water, managers release much of it to nearby coastal estuaries. The Everglades Agricultural Area Reservoir, built to store that water and send it south, is due to be completed in 2029.

Even so, new bridges along the Tamiami Trail, a highway and levee system that for decades blocked water from flowing south into Everglades National Park, are making a difference. About 10 times more water flowed beneath the road from January through July 2026 than in the same months of 2015, despite a harsher drought, according to the Everglades Foundation. That water moves through the park toward the coast, helping keep Florida Bay’s salinity low enough to avoid a repeat of the 2015 seagrass die-off.

“I like wet years, because that’s when we have very productive wildlife years,” Cook said.…

item.title: ‘Vote for trees’: Taiwan community pins hope on ‘Forest Grandma’ to save beloved woods
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Engaging story on community activism with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

- In Kaohsiung’s Ciaotou district, a community is fighting an urban development project that threatens a 154-hectare (380-acre) woodland surrounding the former Ciaotou Sugar Refinery.

- After failing to find politicians to support their fight, they turned to an 83-year-old former factory worker to defend the Ciaotou Woodland, which provides habitat for local wildlife and helps protect the area from flooding.

- Chiang Huang-nu, nicknamed Forest Grandma, is running as an independent candidate in Taiwan’s local elections, with a campaign slogan: “Vote for trees, not for political parties.”

- The push for the development is tied to the growth of the semiconductor industry in southern Taiwan, with the project set to convert a large swath of land around the historic factory into commercial and residential zones for high-tech businesses and their workers.

KAOHSIUNG, Taiwan — At dawn, just as the birds begin to sing, Chiang Huang-nu usually puts on her traditional straw hat and walks through the wooded grounds of a former sugar factory in Ciaotou district in southwest Taiwan. Along the way, the 83-year-old might greet around 30 other regular strollers, most of them retirees.

Chiang has taken these morning walks among the greenery since she was a child. For the past several months, the walk has involved chatting with fellow community members about the community’s fight against the government’s plan to redevelop the area and demolish their beloved wood.

For decades, Chiang and fellow residents have spent their mornings in the Ciaotou Woodland, a 154-hectare (380-acre) urban forest surrounding the historic Ciaotou Sugar Refinery. Located in the eponymous district, north of Kaohsiung city center in southwestern Taiwan, the woodland is home to 100,000 trees, according to local environmentalists, and a habitat for local wildlife.

“Some of the trees were planted during the Japanese colonial period,” which lasted from 1895 to 1945, Chiang told Mongabay. “They are more than 100 years old. They protect us from the heat in summer.”

For the past year, however, residents can only walk in the nearby park. The woodland has been fenced off and made inaccessible to the public, following a government order. Its trees are under threat from the urban redevelopment project.

On a November morning, three elderly men in their 70s were sitting on plastic chairs in the middle of the park, sheltered from the sun by the trees. “I would rather see this place preserved, but what can we do against the government’s decisions?” said one 77-year-old man.

His two companions nodded in agreement.

Faced with such powerlessness, residents have found a glimmer of hope and a figure of resistance in Chiang.

The octogenarian, nicknamed “Forest Grandma” for her passion for protecting the woodland, is running in Taiwan’s local elections on Nov. 28. She is contesting a city council seat in Kaohsiung, the island’s third most populous city. Her only manifesto policy is to protect the wood. Her slogan is “Vote for trees, not parties.”

“Of course I’m going to vote for her,” a 70-year-old resident, who only gave her surname, Tsai, told Mongabay. “If you destroy this forest, what will we have left? We won’t have anywhere to go for a walk.”

Like Chiang, other morning residents on the morning walk come from working-class families. Either they themselves, their parents, or both were employed by the factory, which began operating in 1902. After the sugar refinery ceased operations in 1999, the surrounding area was transformed into a vast woodland.

For around 15 years, the old woodland became a place for many residents from Ciaotou and nearby districts to walk in the mornings or to hike or cycle on weekends.

Forest Grandma has no formal education and is illiterate. She does not speak Mandarin, the official language in Taiwan, and communicates only in Taiwanese Hokkien, the language spoken by descendants of early immigrants from China’s Fujian province who moved to Taiwan centuries ago.

Born into a poor farming family in 1943, during the Japanese colonial rule, she was given a Japanese name, Tamako. Her current name, Huang-nu, was registered after the Nationalist government retreated to Taiwan in 1949, following a civil war in mainland China.

For Chiang Huang-nu, who worked at the Ciaotou Sugar Refinery for years, her political involvement did not stem from an electoral ambition but from a long-standing attachment to a place she has known since her youth. “Destroying this forest means destroying my entire life,” she said.

The idea for her candidacy came from her son, Chiang Yao-hsien, also known as Jungle Chiang. The 68-year-old is a heritage and environmental activist. In 2001, two years after the Ciaotou Sugar Refinery was shut down, he turned the complex into an artists’ village, where his mother volunteers to work as a sweeper.

“My mother is popular in the area,” Chiang Yao-hsien told Mongabay. “Her background as a former factory worker speaks to an entire generation. I knew she could bring people together around our cause. So I encouraged her to run.”

Large-scale urban forest

In 2007, APEC nations made a regional commitment to increase forest cover by 20 million hectares (50 million acres) by 2020. Taiwan pledged to contribute to this goal by increasing its reforested areas by 11,550 hectares (28,540 acres). As part of the commitment, a woodland was planted near Tienpao River in Ciaotou between 2010 and 2012.

Environmentalists praise the woodland as a rare example of a large-scale urban forest in Kaohsiung.

“These trees are not even 20 years old, and today, while we continue to take part in APEC meetings, the authorities are considering destroying this forest for a real estate and land development project,” said Chuang Chieh-jen, chairperson of the Forest City Association, Taiwan (FCAT).…
